title: Mock Exam 42: Dinosaurs, Fossils & Prehistoric Life

listeningParts.title: Booking a fossil-hunting walk
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a coastal visitor centre to book a guided fossil-hunting walk for her family.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Hello, Seacliff Bay Fossil Centre, Tom speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. We're coming to Seacliff Bay on holiday next week, and my kids are obsessed with dinosaurs. I saw on your website that you do guided fossil walks on the beach. Could I book one?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Of course. Our walks are very popular, especially in the school holidays. They're led by one of our geologists, and they last about two hours. Most people find something, usually ammonites, which are the spiral shells of sea creatures that lived here around two hundred million years ago. Occasionally, someone finds a piece of ichthyosaur, a kind of large marine reptile, but I can't promise that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds brilliant. Which days do you run them?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: This month, we run them on Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays. Which day would you like?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Saturday would be best for us.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm sorry, Saturday's fully booked already. We've still got places on Sunday, though.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sunday's fine. What time does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: The start time changes every day, because we can only go out when the tide is low. Otherwise, the sea comes right up to the bottom of the cliffs and it isn't safe. Last week the walks started at eleven, but on Sunday it'll be half past nine in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Half nine. Okay. And where do we meet?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Not here at the centre, but outside the lifeboat station at the eastern end of the beach. The guide will be wearing a bright yellow jacket, so you can't miss her.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: It's twelve pounds for adults and six pounds for children. How many of you will there be?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Two adults and two children. The children are seven and ten. Is that old enough?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, the minimum age is five, and all children must be with an adult at all times. Now, there are a few important safety rules. First, footwear. The rocks can be very slippery, so everyone needs to wear strong boots with a good grip. Please don't come in sandals. And you should bring a waterproof jacket, because the weather can change very quickly on the coast.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Do we need any special equipment? Hammers or anything?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: No, you don't. In fact, we ask people not to use hammers at all. The most important rule is that you must never collect anything from the cliffs themselves. They're very unstable, and rocks fall without warning. The best fossils are actually found lying loose on the beach, where the waves have washed them out. We give each child a small bag to keep their finds in, and an identification chart, so they can work out what they've found.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Lovely. Can we keep what we find?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, as long as it's small and common, like most ammonites. But if anyone finds something rare or scientifically important, we ask them to report it to the centre, so experts can record it. Right, can I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Siobhan Fitzgerald. That's F-I-T-Z-G-E-R-A-L-D.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a phone number, in case we need to cancel because of bad weather?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Great. You can pay when you arrive, by cash or card. And after the walk, I'd recommend coming back here to the centre. We've got a small exhibition of local fossils, and there's a free talk at one o'clock every day about how the cliffs were formed.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll definitely do that. Is there anywhere to park near the lifeboat station?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: There's a small car park there, but it fills up very early. It's usually easier to park at the harbour car park and walk along the seafront, which takes about ten minutes. Oh, and everyone who books a walk gets ten per cent off in our shop, which sells fossils, books and replica dinosaur teeth. The children usually love the teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm sure they will. Thanks very much for your help.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: You're welcome. Enjoy your holiday, and good luck with the fossil hunting.

listeningParts.title: A new dinosaur gallery
listeningParts.contextDescription: A museum volunteer introduces a new gallery about prehistoric life to a group of visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: Hi, everyone, and welcome to the brand-new Age of Giants gallery here at the Riverside Museum. My name's Kelly, and I'm one of the volunteers. The gallery only opened last month, so you're among the first visitors to see it. Before you go in, I'd like to tell you how it was created and what you'll find in each zone.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: The idea for the gallery actually came from our visitors. For years, the most common comment in our visitor book was that people wanted to see more dinosaurs. The old gallery had just two skeletons and a few glass cases, and it hadn't been changed since the 1970s. So, about five years ago, the museum began raising money, and around a third of the cost was donated by members of the public, which we're very grateful for.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: One question people always ask is whether the skeletons are real. The answer is that some are, and some aren't. Real fossil bone is extremely heavy and often fragile, so many museums display casts, which are accurate copies made from the original bones. In this gallery, every label tells you whether you're looking at real fossil material or a cast, so look out for the small red symbol, which means the bones are real.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: The gallery is divided into four zones. The first is the Ocean Zone, which shows life in the seas at the time of the dinosaurs. Many people are surprised to learn that the big sea creatures of that period, such as ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs, weren't dinosaurs at all, but marine reptiles. The centrepiece is a plesiosaur skeleton hanging from the ceiling, and there's a large screen where you can watch an animation of it swimming.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: Next is the Forest Zone, which is the one most children head for first. It's designed to look like a forest from around seventy million years ago, and it contains our star attraction, a full-size Tyrannosaurus rex. It's a cast, I'm afraid, but it's based on one of the most complete skeletons ever found. Here's a fact that people love: Tyrannosaurus actually lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus. The two are often shown together in films, but they were separated by tens of millions of years.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: The third area is the Discovery Lab. This is where you can see how scientists study fossils. Through the large window, you can watch our team cleaning and preparing real fossils, and on weekdays one of the scientists comes out at eleven to answer questions. There are also microscopes you can use yourself, and a sandpit where younger visitors can dig for replica bones.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: Finally, there's the Ice Age Hall, which jumps forward to much more recent times, after the dinosaurs had gone. This is where you'll find the mammals, including a woolly mammoth and a sabre-toothed cat. Most mammoths died out around ten thousand years ago, but a small population survived on an island in the Arctic Ocean until around four thousand years ago. That means some mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid in Egypt was built. In this hall, you can also touch a real mammoth tooth, which is about the size of a shoebox.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: A few practical things. Bags can be left in the lockers by the entrance, which take a one-dollar coin that you get back afterwards. Please don't touch the skeletons, except for the objects marked with a hand symbol. And if you'd like a deeper experience, we offer audio guides, which last about forty minutes and are free for museum members.

dialogue.speaker: Volunteer
dialogue.text: We're also looking for more volunteers, especially people who'd like to help in the Discovery Lab at weekends. No experience is needed, as full training is provided. If you're interested, please ask at the information desk. Right, enjoy the gallery, and don't forget to say hello to the T. rex.

listeningParts.title: Are birds living dinosaurs?
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two biology students, Hana and Owen, discuss their presentation on the evolution of birds with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, Hana, Owen. So, your presentation is on the idea that birds evolved from dinosaurs. How are you getting on?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Pretty well. We've decided to organise it as a story, going through the main discoveries in the order they happened, because the idea has gone in and out of fashion over the last hundred and sixty years.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sorry, I mean, good. Where does the story start?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: With Archaeopteryx. The first skeleton was found in limestone in Germany and described in 1861, only two years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species, in 1859. It had feathers and wings like a bird, but also teeth, claws on its wings and a long bony tail, like a reptile. So it looked exactly like the kind of in-between creature Darwin's theory predicted.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: And soon afterwards, Thomas Henry Huxley pointed out how similar birds were to some small meat-eating dinosaurs. But during the twentieth century the idea lost support. One reason was that dinosaurs didn't seem to have collarbones, which birds have, so scientists thought they couldn't be closely related.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what changed?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Two things, really. First, in the late 1960s, John Ostrom described a dinosaur called Deinonychus, which was clearly an active, fast-moving hunter, and its skeleton was remarkably similar to Archaeopteryx. That made people reconsider. And later, collarbones were found in many dinosaur fossils, so that objection disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Then the really big change came in 1996, in north-east China, with Sinosauropteryx. It was a small dinosaur that couldn't fly, but it was covered in simple, hair-like feathers. Since then, dozens of feathered dinosaurs have been found in the same region.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Why are the Chinese fossils so well preserved?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Because the animals were buried very quickly in fine volcanic ash and mud at the bottom of lakes. The ash was so fine that even soft parts like feathers left impressions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. I'd make sure you explain that clearly, because the audience may wonder why feathers survive in some places but not others. What's your main argument about why feathers evolved?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: This was the part we found most interesting. If many dinosaurs had feathers but couldn't fly, then feathers can't have evolved for flight in the first place. The most likely explanation is that they first helped animals keep warm, and perhaps later they were used for display, to attract mates. Flight came much later.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point. Biologists sometimes say a feature was borrowed for a new purpose. And have you included anything about colour?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Yes. We were amazed that scientists can now tell the colours of some dinosaurs. They use powerful microscopes to look at tiny structures inside fossil feathers that once contained pigment. In 2010, researchers showed that Sinosauropteryx had a tail with reddish-brown and white stripes.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That always gets a reaction from audiences. Now, the presentation is twenty minutes. How are you dividing it?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Hana will do the history, and I'll do the evidence from the Chinese fossils and the colour research. Then we'll finish together with a few minutes on what it all means.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fine. One weakness, though: at the moment, it sounds as if all scientists completely agree. A small number still question parts of the theory, so mention that briefly, to show you've read widely.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Okay, that's fair. What about visuals?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Use a family tree diagram showing where birds fit among the dinosaurs. And I'd avoid putting too much text on your slides. If you can, bring a cast of a fossil for people to look at; the department has several you can borrow.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: That would be great. Could we borrow the Archaeopteryx cast?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'm sure that can be arranged. Ask the technician, and book it at least a week before the presentation.

listeningParts.title: How fossils are formed
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory palaeontology course on the processes that turn living things into fossils.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at how fossils are formed, and why the fossil record gives us such an incomplete picture of past life. The word fossil comes from a Latin word meaning 'dug up', and originally it was used for almost anything taken out of the ground. Today, we use it to mean any preserved evidence of life from the distant past, usually more than about ten thousand years old.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first thing to understand is that fossilisation is extremely rare. When most plants and animals die, they simply disappear. Their bodies are eaten by scavengers, broken down by bacteria, or scattered and worn away by wind and water. Only a tiny fraction of all the living things that have ever existed have become fossils, and only a tiny fraction of those have been found.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what conditions make fossilisation more likely? The most important is rapid burial. If an animal is quickly covered by sediment, such as mud, sand or volcanic ash, it's protected from scavengers, and the supply of oxygen is cut off, which slows down decay. That's why so many fossils come from places that were once at the bottom of seas, lakes or rivers, where sediment builds up steadily. The second factor is the presence of hard parts. Bones, teeth and shells are far more likely to survive than skin, muscles or leaves, so animals with skeletons are much better represented in the fossil record than soft-bodied creatures such as worms or jellyfish.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's look at the main ways fossils form. The most common process is called permineralisation. After burial, groundwater seeps through the sediment and into the tiny spaces inside bone or wood. This water carries dissolved minerals, such as silica or calcite, which slowly crystallise and fill these spaces, turning the original material into stone. Petrified wood, which can preserve the detail of tree rings, is formed in this way.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sometimes, though, the original material dissolves completely, leaving a hollow space in the rock with the exact shape of the organism. This is called a mould. If that space is later filled by other minerals, the result is a cast, which is like a natural copy of the original. Many fossil shells are preserved in this way.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Not all fossils are the remains of bodies. Trace fossils are signs of an organism's activity, such as footprints, burrows, tooth marks and fossilised dung. These can tell us things that bones cannot. For example, long trackways of footprints suggest that some dinosaurs travelled in herds, and the distance between footprints can be used to estimate how fast an animal was moving.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There are also some rare cases of exceptional preservation. Small creatures such as insects and spiders have been trapped in sticky tree resin, which hardened into amber, preserving them in remarkable detail. In the frozen ground of Siberia, woolly mammoths have been found with skin, hair and even stomach contents. And at the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles, thousands of animals, including sabre-toothed cats, became stuck in natural asphalt and were preserved.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Perhaps the most famous site of all is the Burgess Shale, high in the Rocky Mountains of Canada, which was discovered by the American scientist Charles Walcott in 1909. It's around five hundred million years old, and it preserves soft-bodied animals that would normally leave no trace at all, giving us a unique window into early animal life in the oceans.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, fossils are not only useful for studying ancient life; they also help geologists date rocks. Certain species existed for a relatively short time but were widespread, so when they're found in a layer of rock, they show its approximate age. These are known as index fossils, and ammonites are a classic example. Next week, we'll look at how fossils are excavated and prepared in the laboratory.

readingPassages.title: The fossil hunter of Lyme Regis
paragraphs: The small town of Lyme Regis lies on the south coast of England, in the county of Dorset, beneath cliffs made of layers of grey clay and limestone. These rocks formed on the floor of a shallow sea around two hundred million years ago, during the early part of the Jurassic period, and they are packed with fossils. Every winter, storms and heavy rain trigger landslides on the cliffs, exposing new remains on the beach below. It was here, in 1799, that Mary Anning was born. Although she had almost no formal education, she would become one of the most important fossil collectors in the history of science.

The Anning family was poor. Mary's father, Richard, was a cabinetmaker, but he also earned extra money by collecting fossils from the beach and selling them as 'curiosities' to wealthy visitors. Lyme Regis was becoming a fashionable seaside resort at the time, partly because the long wars with France made it difficult for the British upper classes to travel to the continent. A famous story is told about Mary's early life: when she was a baby, she was being held by a woman standing under a tree with two others when lightning struck. The three women were killed, but Mary survived. When Richard Anning died in 1810, he left his family in debt, and selling fossils became an important source of income for his widow and children.

The family's first major discovery came in 1811, when Mary's brother Joseph found the skull of a strange animal in the cliffs. About a year later, Mary, who was then only around twelve years old, found the rest of the skeleton. It was a creature unlike anything most people had seen, with a long jaw full of teeth, large eyes and a body shaped rather like a dolphin's. It was sold to a wealthy collector and later displayed in London, and scientists eventually gave it the name Ichthyosaurus, which means 'fish lizard'.

More remarkable finds followed. In 1823, Mary discovered the first nearly complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a marine reptile with a small head, flippers and an extraordinarily long neck. The neck was so long that the French anatomist Georges Cuvier, the most respected expert of the day, at first suspected that the fossil might be a fake, made by combining bones from different animals. After examining drawings of the specimen more carefully, Cuvier accepted that it was genuine, and the episode greatly increased Mary's reputation among scientists.

In 1828 she found the skeleton of a pterosaur, a flying reptile; it was the first to be discovered outside Germany. She also made an important contribution to the understanding of how ancient animals lived. Collectors had long been puzzled by small stony objects known as 'bezoar stones', which were often found in the region of the abdomen of ichthyosaur skeletons. Mary noticed that when these objects were broken open, they often contained fish bones and scales. The geologist William Buckland concluded that they were fossilised droppings, and in 1829 he named them coprolites. They provided direct evidence of what these animals had eaten.

Fossil hunting was dangerous work. The best time to search was in winter, after storms, when the cliffs were at their most unstable. In 1833, a sudden landslide killed Mary's dog, Tray, which usually accompanied her, and she herself narrowly escaped. Mary was not simply a collector, however. She taught herself anatomy by reading scientific papers, copying their illustrations by hand and dissecting modern fish and cuttlefish to compare them with her fossils. Visitors to her shop were often astonished to find that this working woman understood the subject as well as many professors.

Despite her achievements, Mary Anning received little formal recognition during her lifetime. As a woman, she could not join the Geological Society of London, and the scientists who bought her fossils often published descriptions of them without mentioning who had found them. She also experienced financial hardship, especially after losing much of her savings in a bad investment, and some of her scientific friends arranged for her to receive an annual payment. She died in 1847, aged forty-seven, and after her death the president of the Geological Society paid tribute to her in a speech, an unusual honour for someone who had never been allowed to be a member.

Her reputation has grown steadily since then. In 2010, the Royal Society included her in a list of the ten British women who have most influenced the history of science. In 2022, a statue of her was unveiled in Lyme Regis, following a campaign started by a local schoolgirl. It is often claimed that the tongue-twister 'She sells seashells on the seashore' was inspired by her, but this link has never been proved. What is certain is that the fossils she found helped to convince scientists that the Earth had once been home to creatures very different from those alive today, and that many of them had become extinct.

readingPassages.title: The day the dinosaurs died
paragraphs: Around sixty-six million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous period, life on Earth suffered one of the greatest catastrophes in its history. Roughly three-quarters of all plant and animal species disappeared, including every dinosaur except the ancestors of today's birds. For much of the twentieth century, the cause of this mass extinction was one of the great mysteries of science. Dozens of explanations were proposed, from gradual changes in climate to disease, and even the suggestion that early mammals had eaten too many dinosaur eggs. None of them could be properly tested.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected direction. In the 1970s, the American geologist Walter Alvarez was studying rocks near the town of Gubbio in central Italy, where a thin layer of clay marks the boundary between the Cretaceous rocks and the younger rocks above. He wanted to know how long the clay had taken to form. His father, Luis Alvarez, a Nobel Prize-winning physicist, suggested measuring the amount of iridium in it. Iridium is extremely rare in the Earth's crust but more common in meteorites, and tiny amounts fall from space at a fairly steady rate, so the quantity in the clay should indicate how long it had taken to build up. To their surprise, the clay contained many times more iridium than expected. Similar results soon came from sites in Denmark and New Zealand.

In 1980, the Alvarezes and two chemists, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel, published a bold explanation. They argued that the iridium had come from an asteroid around ten kilometres wide, which had struck the Earth and thrown enormous quantities of dust into the atmosphere. Many palaeontologists were deeply sceptical. For more than a century, geologists had been taught that the Earth changes slowly and gradually, and the idea of a sudden catastrophe from space seemed to belong to science fiction rather than science. There was also an obvious problem: if such an impact had happened, where was the crater?

The answer had, in fact, already been found, although few people knew it. In the late 1970s, geophysicists working for Mexico's state oil company had detected a huge circular structure buried beneath the Yucatán Peninsula, but their findings received little attention. In 1991, a team of researchers showed that this structure, now known as the Chicxulub crater, was about the right age and size. It is around one hundred and eighty kilometres wide and lies hidden beneath hundreds of metres of younger rock. Grains of shocked quartz, which form only under extreme pressure, and tiny glassy beads created from melted rock were found in boundary layers around the Gulf of Mexico, strengthening the case.

Scientists have since pieced together what probably happened. The impact released more than a billion times the energy of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima. Huge tsunamis swept across the surrounding seas, and hot debris thrown into the atmosphere fell back across large parts of the planet, possibly starting widespread fires. Worse still, the asteroid struck rocks rich in sulphur, sending vast amounts of sulphur gases and soot into the upper atmosphere. These blocked sunlight for months or even years, causing global temperatures to fall sharply. Without sunlight, plants and tiny ocean organisms could not grow, and food chains collapsed from the bottom upwards.

Not all scientists accept that the asteroid acted alone. At around the same time, a series of enormous volcanic eruptions was taking place in western India, producing lava flows that today form a region known as the Deccan Traps. Over hundreds of thousands of years, these eruptions released huge quantities of carbon dioxide and sulphur gases, which may have already been disturbing the climate and putting ecosystems under stress before the asteroid arrived. The precise timing of the eruptions is still debated, but many researchers now believe that the impact was the main cause of the extinction, while the volcanoes may have made matters worse.

Just as interesting as the question of why so many species died is the question of why others survived. Survivors tended to be small, which meant they needed less food, and many could shelter from the worst conditions in burrows or in water. Animals with varied diets, able to eat insects, seeds or decaying material, also did better than specialists. Crocodiles, turtles, many small mammals and some birds, probably those living on the ground, all came through the crisis. Life in freshwater was generally less affected than life on land, perhaps because many freshwater food chains depended on dead plant material rather than on living plants.

For the survivors, the disappearance of the dinosaurs created enormous opportunities. Mammals, which had lived alongside dinosaurs for over a hundred million years but had mostly remained small, spread rapidly into the habitats that had been left empty, and within a few million years they had become much larger and more varied. Without this disaster, it is unlikely that humans would ever have evolved. In 2016, an international expedition drilled into the Chicxulub crater itself, recovering rock samples that are helping scientists to understand both the impact and how quickly life returned to the area afterwards.

readingPassages.title: Should we bring back the mammoth?
paragraphs: For most of human history, extinction has been permanent. Once the last member of a species dies, it is gone forever. Recent advances in genetics, however, have led some scientists to suggest that this may no longer be true. The idea of 'de-extinction', bringing extinct species back to life, has moved from science fiction towards the laboratory, and companies and research groups are now working on projects to revive animals such as the woolly mammoth. The question is no longer only whether this can be done, but whether it should be.

The first, and so far only, animal to be brought back from extinction, at least briefly, was the Pyrenean ibex, a wild mountain goat from the border between Spain and France. The last known individual, a female, was killed by a falling tree in 2000, but scientists had already taken and frozen samples of her skin cells. In 2003, they used these cells to produce a clone, which was carried by a goat. The baby ibex was born alive, but it died within minutes because of a serious defect in its lungs. The experiment showed both what might be possible and how difficult it would be.

The best-known project today aims to recreate the woolly mammoth. Most mammoths died out around ten thousand years ago, though a small population survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, until around four thousand years ago. Because mammoth remains have been preserved in frozen ground, scientists have been able to read much of the animal's genetic code. The plan is not to clone a mammoth, since no living cells survive, but to edit the genes of its closest living relative, the Asian elephant, adding mammoth features such as thick hair and a layer of fat to protect against the cold. The result would then need to be carried by an elephant mother, or perhaps one day grown in an artificial womb, and elephant pregnancies last around twenty-two months.

Supporters argue that such animals could benefit the environment. In northern Siberia, the Russian scientist Sergey Zimov has created an area known as Pleistocene Park, where he hopes to show that large grazing animals can turn mossy forest back into grassland. Some researchers suggest that herds of mammoth-like elephants, by trampling snow and knocking down trees, might help to keep the frozen ground below, known as permafrost, from thawing and releasing greenhouse gases. Others have proposed reviving the passenger pigeon, a North American bird whose flocks once numbered in the billions before hunting and forest clearance wiped it out, and whose last member, Martha, died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Similar plans exist for the thylacine, a striped meat-eating marsupial from Tasmania, the last known individual of which died in a zoo in 1936.

Not every extinct animal could be brought back, however. Films may have encouraged the idea that dinosaurs could be recreated from ancient DNA, but this is not possible. DNA breaks down over time, even in ideal conditions. A 2012 study of fossil bones from the moa, a giant extinct bird from New Zealand, estimated that half of the chemical bonds in a DNA sample break down roughly every five hundred years. The oldest DNA ever recovered is around two million years old, while the last non-avian dinosaurs died sixty-six million years ago.

There are also serious scientific doubts about the projects that are possible. An elephant with mammoth genes would not truly be a mammoth, and nobody knows how such an animal would behave without parents of its own kind to learn from. Elephants are highly social animals, and raising a lonely individual in a laboratory raises obvious welfare concerns. Moreover, a revived species would need a suitable habitat, yet the very conditions that caused many extinctions, such as hunting and the loss of habitat, have not gone away.

Some of the techniques being developed may nevertheless help species that are not yet extinct. The northern white rhino, for example, now has only two surviving members, both of them female, and scientists are attempting to use eggs taken from them and frozen sperm from males that have died to produce embryos, which could be carried by a related rhino. Genetic tools might also be used to increase the genetic diversity of small, isolated populations, or to make animals more resistant to disease.

In my view, the strongest argument against de-extinction is a practical one. Conservation budgets are limited, and the money spent on reviving a handful of lost species might achieve far more if it were used to protect the thousands of species that are threatened today. There is also a risk that the promise of de-extinction will make extinction seem less serious, as if any loss could later be reversed. That said, I do not believe that the research should be abandoned. If the technology helps to save animals such as the northern white rhino, it will have been worthwhile, even if no mammoth ever walks the Siberian plains again.
